questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Compare and contrast the crystallography of the Hexagonal system and the Trigonal system.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **Hexagonal** and **Trigonal** systems are closely related. Both are referred to **four crystallographic axes** (Bravais-Miller axes), and the trigonal system is often treated as a division of the hexagonal family (the rhombohedral lattice).

**Similarities.**
- Both have **four axes**: three horizontal axes $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$ of **equal length**, in one plane, **intersecting at 120 degrees**, and a fourth axis $c$ of **different length**, **perpendicular** to the plane of the other three.
- Axial notation for both: $a_1 = a_2 = a_3 \neq c$; angles between the horizontal axes $120^\circ$ and between $c$ and the horizontal axes $90^\circ$.
- Both are **optically uniaxial** (one optic axis, along $c$).

**Differences.**

| Feature | Hexagonal system | Trigonal system |
|---|---|---|
| Principal axis of symmetry | **Hexad (six-fold) axis** along $c$: the crystal is brought into coincidence with itself 6 times in a turn of 360 degrees | **Triad (three-fold) axis** along $c$ (3 times in a turn of 360 degrees) |
| Highest symmetry class | Dihexagonal dipyramidal ($6/m\,2/m\,2/m$): 1 hexad axis, 6 diad axes, 7 planes of symmetry and a centre | Ditrigonal scalenohedral ($\bar{3}\,2/m$): 1 triad (inverse) axis, 3 diad axes, 3 planes of symmetry and a centre |
| Cross-section normal to $c$ | **Hexagonal** (six sides) | Triangular, or hexagonal with unequal alternate faces (trigonal) |
| Typical forms | Hexagonal prism, hexagonal dipyramid and basal pinacoid | Rhombohedron, scalenohedron, trigonal prism and trigonal pyramid |
| Alternative axes | Only the four-axis (hexagonal) system | Can also be referred to **three equal axes inclined at an equal angle other than 90 degrees** ($a = b = c$, $\alpha = \beta = \gamma \neq 90^\circ$): the **rhombohedral** lattice |
| Examples | **Beryl**, **apatite**, **nepheline**, graphite, covellite | **Calcite**, **quartz** (low quartz), **dolomite**, hematite, corundum, tourmaline |

**Sketch.** Draw the four axes: $c$ vertical, and $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$ in a horizontal plane at 120 degrees to each other, each labelled with its positive end. A hexagonal prism (beryl) with the basal pinacoid, drawn on these axes, and a rhombohedron (calcite) with a triad axis through opposite corners, show the difference of symmetry.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Describe the following physical properties as used in the identification of minerals:

(i) Colour;  (4 marks)

(ii) Streak;  (2 marks)

(iii) Hardness.  (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Colour (4 marks).** Colour is the **appearance of the mineral in reflected light, as seen on a fresh surface in a hand specimen**. It depends on the **chemical composition** and on the way the mineral absorbs some wavelengths of light.
- In **idiochromatic** minerals the colour is a property of the mineral and is constant, because it is due to an essential element (Fe, Cu...): malachite is always green, azurite blue, sulphur yellow, magnetite black.
- In **allochromatic** minerals the colour is due to **small impurities** or defects in the crystal lattice, so that the same mineral has many colours: quartz may be colourless (rock crystal), purple (amethyst, iron), pink (rose quartz) or smoky; corundum is red (ruby, chromium) or blue (sapphire, iron and titanium); beryl is green (emerald, chromium).
- Colour is therefore a **useful but not a reliable** property for identification, especially for light-coloured minerals; weathering or tarnish may change the surface colour, so a fresh surface must be examined. It is more reliable for opaque minerals with metallic lustre.

**(ii) Streak (2 marks).** Streak is the **colour of the fine powder of a mineral**, observed when it is rubbed on a plate of **unglazed porcelain (streak plate)**. It is **more constant and so more reliable than the colour of the specimen**: hematite is black, grey or reddish but has a **red-brown streak**; pyrite (brass yellow) has a **greenish-black streak**; galena has a grey-black streak; gold a golden-yellow streak; calcite and quartz a white streak. Minerals **harder than the plate** (about 6.5) leave no streak (powder), and the test is used mainly with metallic and coloured minerals.

**(iii) Hardness (4 marks).** Hardness is the **resistance of a mineral to scratching (abrasion)**. It depends on the **strength of the chemical bonds** and the packing of the atoms in the crystal lattice, and it is measured on **Mohs' scale**, a **relative scale of ten minerals** (1 talc, 2 gypsum, 3 calcite, 4 fluorite, 5 apatite, 6 orthoclase, 7 quartz, 8 topaz, 9 corundum, 10 diamond), where a mineral scratches all those with a lower number. In the field the mineral is tried against the **fingernail (about 2.5)**, a **copper coin (about 3.5)**, a **steel knife blade or glass (about 5.5)** and a **steel file or the streak plate (about 6.5)**. A fresh, unweathered surface is used, and the mineral is scratched with a pointed corner of the reference. Hardness may vary with direction in some crystals (kyanite is 4.5 along the length and 6.5 across), and it must not be confused with toughness or brittleness.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) With named examples of rocks, outline foliated textures in metamorphic rocks.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Foliation** is the **planar arrangement (parallel alignment) of platy and elongate minerals**, such as micas, chlorite and amphibole, produced when rocks are recrystallised under **directed pressure (differential stress)** in **regional metamorphism**. The foliated textures increase in grain size with the grade of metamorphism:

1. **Slaty cleavage: slate.** Very fine-grained (the grains cannot be seen); the rock splits into thin, flat sheets along the cleavage planes, which are **perpendicular to the compression**. It is formed from shale or mudstone at **low grade** (example: **slate**, used for roofing).
2. **Phyllitic texture: phyllite.** Fine-grained, with a **silky or satin sheen** on the cleavage surfaces due to tiny aligned mica crystals; slightly **coarser than slate** (example: **phyllite**).
3. **Schistosity: schist.** Medium- to coarse-grained, with **visible platy minerals (mica, chlorite, talc) arranged in parallel**, so that the rock splits into irregular flakes; it often contains porphyroblasts of garnet, staurolite or kyanite (examples: **mica schist**, garnet schist, hornblende schist), at **medium grade**.
4. **Gneissic banding: gneiss.** Coarse-grained, with **alternating light bands (quartz and feldspar) and dark bands (biotite, hornblende)**, at **high grade** (examples: **granite gneiss** from granite or **banded gneiss** from sediments).
